accroche: Most dated diamonds are older than the first land plant.
contenu_vulgarise:
In many textbooks and popular-science videos, the explanation fits in one sentence: a diamond is a piece of coal that, buried deep enough and long enough, ended up crystallizing under pressure. The image appeals because it links two familiar carbon materials, one black and cheap, the other transparent and precious. Yet it is wrong on almost every point.

## A question of depth

Most natural gem-quality diamonds form at the base of old continents, between 150 and 200 kilometers deep, where pressure and a temperature of at least 1,050 °C allow carbon to crystallize in this particular form rather than as graphite. Coal, for its part, is a sedimentary rock: it forms through the burial of plant matter in a basin, rarely at more than 3.2 kilometers deep. Beyond that, heat destroys its structure long before it approaches the conditions for diamond. The two materials occupy geological levels that do not communicate: nothing in the workings of the Earth's crust buries a coal deposit all the way to the mantle.

## A problem of timing

The second problem is dates. Coal requires land plants to bury, and the first of them appear on Earth only about 450 million years ago. Yet a good share of the diamonds mined today are far older than that. Inclusions found in South African diamonds have been dated to as much as 2.6 billion years by researchers at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. According to geology.com, most dated diamonds are far older than the first land plants: they therefore cannot come from coal.

## What this shifts

The carbon in diamonds therefore comes from much older and deeper reservoirs: carbon trapped in the mantle since the early days of the Earth, or recycled over hundreds of millions of years by the subduction of oceanic crust. A diamond is a witness to depth, on an entirely different timescale than coal. The confusion probably comes from a correct chemical intuition (carbon can indeed crystallize into diamond under pressure) applied in the wrong place. The pressure that matters is not the one you reach by digging. It is that of the mantle, a hundred and fifty kilometers beneath your feet.

repere.texte: Gem diamonds crystallize between 150 and 200 km deep; coal rarely goes below 3.2 km. Some inclusions in South African diamonds are dated to 2.6 billion years, well before the first land plants, which appeared about 450 million years ago.
repere.source: GIA, Gems & Gemology (2018); Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, Columbia Climate School (2021)

carte.punch: Most dated diamonds are older than the first plants.
carte.idee: Diamond is explained as compressed coal. But coal stays a few kilometers deep, whereas diamond crystallizes at 150-200 km. Most dated diamonds are older than the first land plants, which appeared about 450 million years ago.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Myth: Can Diamonds Be Made From Coal?
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A short, general-audience version of the same argument, including the timeline of land plants.

quiz.question: Why can't most diamonds come from compressed coal?
choix: Because coal is too hard a material to turn into diamond
Because coal never goes down to the depths and pressures where diamonds form
Because diamonds contain a different type of carbon than coal
Because coal takes longer to form than diamonds
quiz.explication: Coal is a sedimentary rock that is rarely buried beyond a few kilometers, whereas diamonds crystallize at 150-200 km deep. Many diamonds are also far older than the first land plants, which are nonetheless the raw material of coal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: At what depth do most natural gem-quality diamonds form?
choix: Between 150 and 200 kilometers, at the base of old continents
Between 3 and 10 kilometers, in ancient sedimentary basins
At the surface, during the rapid cooling of lava
At more than 500 kilometers, in the Earth's outer core
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gem diamonds crystallize between 150 and 200 km deep, at the base of old continents, where the temperature reaches at least 1,050 degrees Celsius.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the carbon that forms diamonds actually come from?
choix: From the recent decomposition of buried plants and animals
From carbon trapped in the mantle since the early days of the Earth, or recycled by subduction
From carbon-rich meteorites that fell to the surface
From the incomplete combustion of coal under very high pressure
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The carbon in diamonds comes from ancient, deep reservoirs, trapped in the mantle since the Earth's origin or recycled over hundreds of millions of years by the subduction of oceanic crust.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the dating of inclusions found in South African diamonds reveal?
choix: That they formed after the appearance of the first land plants
That they date from about 450 million years ago, like the oldest coal
That they can reach 2.6 billion years, well before the first plants
That they cannot be dated with current methods
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Researchers at the Lamont-Doherty Observatory dated some inclusions to as much as 2.6 billion years, well before the first land plants, which appeared about 450 million years ago.
